THIS CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION HAVING COME UP FOR ADMISSION ON 29.07.2025, THE COURT ON THE SAME DAY DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 Crl.R.P.No.1688 of 2016  2  2025:KER
ORDER The revision petitioners are accused Nos.1 and 2 respectively in ST No.290 of 2009 on the files of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Vaikom.

entities.text: Judicial First Class Magistrate Court, Vaikom
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. The case arose on a complaint filed by the Food Inspector, Ettumanoor Circle against accused,
three in number, alleging commission of offences punishable under Sections 16(1) a(i), 16(1)a(ii) r/w Section 2(ia)a, 2(ix)k, 7(i) & 7(ii) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Act' for short) and Rule 5 Appendix B, A 17-11 and Rule 32(e),(f) and (i) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Rules' for short).

entities.text: Rule 5 Appendix B, A 17-11 and Rule 32(e),(f) and (i)
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text: 3. The prosecution case is that on 08.07.2008 at about 06:30 p.m., PW1, who is the food inspector of Ettumannoor Circle, inspected the shop named Anand Oil Industries, Thottakom and purchased 750 gms of gingelly oil kept in a tin of 15 kg named, 'Aiswarya Nallenna'.

The oil which PW1 purchased from the shop was divided into three equal parts and filled in three steriled plastic containers of 250 gm each and sampled in 2025:KER:56114 accordance with the PFA Act and Rules.

One of the samples was sent to the Public Analyst, who after analysis reported that the sample does not conform to the standard prescribed for Til oil (gingelly oil) falling under item No. A-17-11 of Appendix B of the PFA Rules and is not labelled in accordance with the Rule 32(e),
(f) and (i) of PFA Rules.

entities.text: item No. A-17-11 of Appendix B
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text: The 2 nd accused is alleged to be the licensee of the shop and the 3 rd accused is the person from whom the gingelly oil was allegedly purchased by the 1 st accused.
4. In the trial court, from the side of the complainant, PW1 to PW6 were examined, and Ext.P1 to P31 documents were marked.
When the accused were examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C., they denied all the incriminating circumstances appearing against them in evidence and contended that they are innocent.
From the side of the accused, the 1 st accused was examined as DW1 and Ext.D1 document was marked.

The trial court, on an appreciation of the evidence on record, found all the accused guilty of the offences under Section 16(1)(a)(i) r/w Section 2(ia) a, 2(ix) k, 7(i) and 7(ii) of T.V.Aniyan vs Food Inspector on 29 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/138527100/
2 PFA Act, 1954 and Rule 5 Appendix B, A 17-11 and Rule 32(e),(f) and (i) of PFA Rules, 1955 and convicted them thereunder.

entities.text: Rule 5 Appendix B, A 17-11 and Rule 32(e),(f) and (i)
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text:
The accused were sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of six months and to pay a fine of Rs.1000/- each for the offence under Section 16(i)
2025:KER:56114 (a)(i) of PFA Act, with a default clause.
But the trial court acquitted the accused of the offence under Section 16(i)(a)(ii) of PFA Act.
5. The 1st and the 2nd accused carried the matter in appeal by filing Crl.Appl.No. 47 of 2013 before the Sessions Court, Kottayam.
The said court vide judgment dated 08.09.2016 allowed the appeal in part.

Even though, it found that the prosecution has failed to prove the allegation of adulteration,
found that the accused are guilty of the offence under Rule 32 (e), (f) and (i) of the PFA Rules for misbranding and upheld the sentence imposed by the trial court under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of PFA Act.
6. Heard Sri. Santhosh Subramanian, the learned counsel for the revision petitioners, Sri. Grashious Kuriakose, the learned Additional Director General of Prosecution for the State and Sri.
Ananthkrishnan A. Kartha, the learned Amicus Curie.
7. It is submitted by the learned counsel for the revision petitioners that the 1st revision petitioner/the 1st accused had died during the pendency of this revision petition.

He argued that both the trial court and the appellate court have failed to appreciate the evidence in a proper perspective and has arrived 2025:KER:56114 at a wrong conclusion of guilt against the accused.
He submitted that the revision petitioners are in no way connected with the printing and affixing of labels, and they have only procured the article from the 3rd accused.
He also submitted that there is no convincing evidence to prove misbranding, as alleged by the prosecution.

8. The learned Amicus Curie, after citing the relevant provisions of the PFA Act, contended that the act is totally silent as to whether a food inspector can prefer a complaint alleging adulteration or misbranding.

He submitted that going by Section 20 of the PFA Act, the complaint, if any, can be lodged only on the basis of a report from the public analyst and the prescribed form for the complaint also supports the same.

But, by relying on the decision in Rasheed N.K. v. Food Inspector,
Thalassery and Another [2016(2) KHC 679], he also submitted that in many cases of misbranding and other offences, there is no need for a report from the Public Analyst for initiation of prosecution and if so, in the instant case, leaving apart, Ext.P14 report, the prosecution can be sustained.
9.

entities.text:
Rasheed N.K. v. Food Inspector,
Thalassery and Another [2016(2) KHC 679]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Sri. Grashious Kuriakose, the learned Additional Director General of Prosecution appearing for the State, by relying on Section 10(4) of the PFA Act, submitted that even in 2025:KER:56114 cases of misbranding, a sample has to be taken and the same has to be submitted for analysis by a public analyst, and a report obtained for initiating prosecution under Section 20 of the Act.

He fairly submitted that in the instant case, the prosecution has mainly relied upon Ext.P14 report of the Public Analyst to file a complaint regarding misbranding and that there is nothing apart from the Ext.P14 report to prove the case of misbranding.

He, by relying on decision in Pepsico India T.V.Aniyan vs Food Inspector on 29 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/138527100/
3 Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector & another [2010 (4) KHC 767], fairly submitted that since no rules have been framed for defining the laboratories where samples of food could be analyzed and since there is no prescribed validated method for analysis, no reliance can be placed upon Ext.P14 to reach a finding regarding misbranding.

entities.text:
Pepsico India T.V.Aniyan vs Food Inspector on 29 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/138527100/
3
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector & another [2010 (4) KHC 767]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 10. In the present case, it is to be seen that the prosecution has been initiated against the accused for committing the offences of both adulteration and misbranding.

The materials on record show that even though the trial court has convicted all the accused for committing adulteration and misbranding, the appellate court has acquitted the accused of the allegation that they have committed acts of adulteration.
The evidence on record shows that the complaint has been filed by PW1 alleging adulteration and misbranding on the basis of 2025:KER:56114 Ext.P14 report from the public analyst.

It is alleged in the complaint that as per the report received from the Public Analyst,
the sample does not conform to the standard prescribed for til oil (gingelly oil) and that it is not labelled in accordance with Rule 32(e),(f) and (i) of the PFA Rules, 1955.

As held by the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. case (supra), no reliance can be placed upon the Ext. P14 report since, no rules have been framed defining the laboratories where samples of food could be analysed and since, no validated methods of analysis have been prescribed.
If that be so, I have no hesitation in finding that the prosecution for misbranding lodged against the accused, relying upon Ext. P14 report, cannot be sustained.
11. There is also one other reason that justifies the afore conclusion.
As stated earlier, the prosecution has been lodged on the basis of Ext.P14, alleging that the gingelly oil seized from the accused does not conform to the standard prescribed in the PFA Act.
If so, once it is found that Ext.P14 report cannot be relied upon, there are no other convincing materials to show that the article thus seized is a food article or not.

In other words, if there is no convincing evidence to show that the article seized is a food article, there is no question of any compliance with Rule 32(e),(f) and (i) of the PFA Rules, which speaks about labelling of 2025:KER:56114 food articles in a prescribed manner.
For this ground also, I find that prosecution against the accused for misbranding will not lie.

12. In the light of the afore discussions, I find that the appellate court has not properly appreciated the materials on record and the relevant provisions of the law while reaching a conclusion of guilt against the accused.
This in turn means that this revision petition is only to be allowed, thereby setting aside the conviction and sentence against the revision petitioners/accused Nos.1 and 2.
